title: Immunobiology: An Introduction
summary: Immunity is the capacity of the body to recognise foreign material and neutralise, eliminate or metabolise it. Immunobiology is the study of the immune system. Edward Jenner (1749-1823) is the father of modern immunobiology: milkmaids who recovered from cowpox did not get smallpox, hence vaccination (vacca = cow). The immune system distinguishes 'self' from 'non-self'. Defence mechanisms: physical or anatomical barriers, metabolic defence, immunological defence (the most important: protects against viruses, bacteria, fungi, parasites and tumours, removes damaged cells and maintains homeostasis) and other cellular defences.

Lymphoid organs: central or primary (thymus and bone marrow) and peripheral or secondary (spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches and MALT). Cells: lymphocytes and macrophages (from monocytes), all derived from stem cells of the bone marrow. B-cells (B for bursa of Fabricius): mature in the bone marrow, have surface immunoglobulin that acts as the receptor for a specific antigen, produce antibodies after turning into plasma cells and also form memory cells that respond quickly to the same antigen later. T-cells (T for thymus): mature in the thymus; regulate the immune response, mediate cell-mediated immunity and induce B-cells to make antibodies; helper T-cells (TH) promote B-cell and T-cell activity, cytotoxic T-cells (TC) kill virus-infected and tumour cells and suppressor T-cells (TS) limit the response.

An antigen is any foreign molecule (usually proteins or large polysaccharides) that triggers a specific immune response; an immunogen provokes the response; the part of the antigen that contacts the antibody is the epitope and the part of the antibody that binds is the paratope. An antibody is a protein (immunoglobulin) made in response to an antigen: four polypeptide chains, two heavy and two light chains joined by disulphide bonds, shaped like a Y with a constant stem (Fc) and two variable prongs forming the specific antigen-binding sites. Five classes: IgG (75 per cent of the total; crosses the placenta), IgM, IgA (in milk, colostrum and mucosa), IgD and IgE (allergy). Plasma cells (differentiated B-cells) make antibodies, which bind antigens and lead to clumping (agglutination), neutralisation, and phagocytosis of the antigen.

Immune responses: non-specific (phagocytosis by macrophages and microphages; the complement system of at least 20 proteins, C3 being most abundant, which kills microbes and acts as opsonin) and specific or adaptive: cell-mediated (by cytotoxic T-cells and natural killer cells; against intracellular viruses, cancer cells and transplanted tissue) and humoral or antibody-mediated (by plasma cells; against bacteria and viruses and their toxins). Both are helped by helper T-cells and inhibited by suppressor T-cells.

Innate (natural) immunity: first line of defence; physical barriers (skin made of keratin, with acidic lactic acid secretion by sebaceous glands; mucus and cilia in the respiratory tract; epithelial linings; sweat, tears, HCl in gastric juice, spermine); phagocytic cells; and the complement system. Acquired immunity: active (after infection, e.g. lifelong after diphtheria, whooping cough, smallpox and mumps, short-lived after cold and influenza; or by vaccination) and passive (antibodies transferred ready-made: from mother to foetus across the placenta or through colostrum and breast milk, or by injecting serum or pooled immunoglobulin).

Active immunisation (vaccination): introduces attenuated or killed germs so that the body produces memory cells for quick response on re-exposure (Jenner 1796). Types: killed organisms (typhoid, cholera, pertussis, rabies, polio injection), live attenuated organisms (BCG, rubella, measles, oral polio) and toxoids (modified, harmless toxins such as in diphtheria and tetanus). BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guerin) is for tuberculosis; DPT is a triple vaccine against diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough) and tetanus; MMR is against measles, mumps and rubella. Passive immunisation: ready-made antibodies such as anti-tetanus serum and anti-snake venom give immediate but temporary protection.

objective: Name the type of immunity: (a) transfer of IgG from mother to foetus (b) vaccination with BCG.
State true or false: (a) B-cells mature in the thymus. (b) Memory cells give a quick response to a second exposure to an antigen.
Name the three types of T-cells.
Helper T-cells (TH), cytotoxic T-cells (TC) and suppressor T-cells (TS).
Match: (a) Plasma cells (b) Cytotoxic T-cells (c) Macrophages with (i) antibodies (ii) phagocytosis (iii) kill infected cells.
(a) Bacillus Calmette-Guerin. (b) Measles, Mumps and Rubella.
Name two live attenuated vaccines and two killed vaccines.
Live: BCG and measles; killed: typhoid and rabies.
Name the two types of specific immune responses.
Name two primary and two secondary lymphoid organs.
Primary: thymus and bone marrow; secondary: spleen and lymph nodes.
vsa: Self is the body's own tissues; non-self is foreign material such as pathogens that the immune system recognises and attacks.
Differentiate between B-cells and T-cells (two points).
B-cells mature in the bone marrow and produce antibodies (humoral); T-cells mature in the thymus and mediate cell-mediated immunity.
What is an antigen? Name its parts which contact the antibody.
A foreign molecule that triggers a specific immune response; the epitope is the part that contacts the antibody paratope.
A group of at least 20 plasma proteins that kill microbes without phagocytosis and help phagocytosis (opsonins).
B-cells that do not become plasma cells and remain to produce antibodies quickly if the antigen appears again.
State the difference between active and passive immunity.
Active: the body produces its own antibodies after infection or vaccination, long lasting; passive: ready-made antibodies are received, short-lived.
A chemically or physically modified toxin which is no longer harmful but remains immunogenic, used in vaccines against diphtheria and tetanus.
Write any two physical barriers of innate immunity.
The keratinised skin with acidic secretions and the mucus with cilia in the respiratory tract.
sa: Explain the structure of an antibody.
A Y-shaped immunoglobulin with two heavy and two light chains joined by disulphide bonds; the stem (Fc) is constant while the two prongs have variable antigen-binding sites.
Distinguish between cell-mediated and humoral immune responses (three points).
Cell-mediated: by T-cells, kills virus-infected and cancer cells and rejects grafts, no antibodies; humoral: by antibodies from plasma cells, acts on bacteria, toxins and free viruses.
Describe the innate immunity and its first line of defence.
Physical barriers (skin, mucus, cilia, secretions), phagocytic cells and complement proteins.
Attenuated or killed germs are introduced; the body produces specific memory cells; on later exposure it responds rapidly with antibodies.
Regulate immune responses; helper T-cells activate B-cells and T-cells; cytotoxic T-cells kill infected and tumour cells; suppressor T-cells limit the response.
IgG (75 per cent, crosses the placenta), IgM, IgA (in secretions and milk), IgD and IgE (allergy).
la: Describe the cells of the immune system.
Lymphocytes (B-cells and T-cells with their origin, maturation and functions), macrophages and plasma and memory cells.
Explain the types of immunity with examples.
Innate (barriers, phagocytes, complement) and acquired (active by infection or vaccine; passive by antibodies from the mother or serum).
Describe antigens and antibodies and the types of immune response.
Antigen properties and epitopes; antibody structure and classes; non-specific and specific (cell-mediated and humoral) responses.
Describe the types of vaccines with examples, with BCG, DPT and MMR.
Killed, live attenuated and toxoid vaccines; BCG for TB, DPT for diphtheria, pertussis and tetanus, MMR for measles, mumps and rubella.
